title: One more year (Luke 13:6–9)
hook: a fruitless fig tree gets another year of digging and dung

segments.voice: Yesterday, ravens with no barns and lilies that never spin. Your line was fear not, little flock.

A tomato plant that never sets fruit. A rosebush that just sits there, green and stubborn, year after year. At some point you stand over it with the shovel and decide: that's it, it's coming out, and something useful is going in. Jesus tells a story about exactly that moment: an owner, a fig tree, and a gardener who asks for one thing before the shovel comes down. It's four verses long.
screen: `THE PLANT THAT NEVER FRUITS.` → `STANDING THERE WITH THE SHOVEL.` → `A GARDENER ASKS FOR ONE THING.`

segments.voice: The setting matters. Just before this, people tell Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate while offering sacrifice, and he mentions eighteen people crushed when a tower fell at Siloam. Were they worse sinners than everyone else? No, he says, but unless you repent, you'll all likewise perish. It's a warning. Then the parable. A man has a fig tree planted in his vineyard. For three years he's come looking for figs and found none. Cut it down, he tells the dresser of the vineyard. Why should it take up the ground? The dresser answers: "Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig about it, and dung it." If it bears fruit, good. If not, then cut it down. And there the story stops. Luke never tells us what happened to the tree; the listener is left standing in the open door. Look at what the gardener does. He doesn't just ask for time. He promises work: digging around the roots so water can reach them, and spreading manure, the least glamorous job in any garden. Mercy here isn't looking the other way. It's getting your hands dirty for something that hasn't earned it. Some Christian readers, Catholic preachers among them, hear the owner as the Father and the gardener as Christ, who pleads for more time and does the digging himself. Others hear it more simply: God is patient, and patience has a deadline. Both keep the warning and the mercy together: the tree still needs to bear fruit, but it gets another year, and somebody to tend it.
screen: `THE TOWER AT SILOAM.` · `THREE YEARS, NO FIGS.` · `DIG ABOUT IT, AND DUNG IT.` · `THE STORY ENDS OPEN.` · then, large: `LET IT ALONE THIS YEAR ALSO.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you're close to giving up on, a friend who keeps canceling, a coworker who hasn't changed, maybe yourself, and picture them as the fig tree, with you standing there holding the shovel. Then picture the gardener's choice instead: one more year, and some digging around the roots, a conversation, a little help, a little less judgment. If you pray, pray for them.
Fig tree. Fruitless three years, until a gardener pleads for one more year of digging and manure before anyone cuts it down. Today's word.
Your line: let it alone this year. Mercy with its sleeves rolled up. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the fig tree at Mass during Lent in the year of Luke's Gospel, a season the Church treats as a time of repentance and of God's patience.

Yes, it still bore nothing, so the owner cut it down the next spring.
